Analogue signals and data acquisition

Signal conditioning for water and environmental measurements

Francesco Ferri
9th semester · Water and Environment Engineering

Lecture 1 · 2 hours + 2-hour exercise

Ask what can go wrong between a physical quantity and the number saved on a computer. Use one student example before continuing.

What you should be able to do

  • Explain how a sensor signal becomes a measurement in engineering units.
  • Choose a sensible gain, voltage range and sampling rate.
  • Recognise clipping, aliasing, offset and noise.
  • Calibrate a load-cell scale and check it with independent masses.

These are the outcomes for today. Students do not need a background in electronics. Keep detailed filter design in the appendix.

Today’s programme

TimeTopic
0–15 minMeasurement chain and sensors
15–40 minConditioning and calibration
40–60 minDAQ, resolution and wiring
60–70 minBreak
70–100 minSampling, noise and filters
100–120 minMeasurement decisions and exercise briefing

The timetable includes short questions and worked calculations. The practical exercise is a separate 120-minute session.

Measurements in our two systems

  • Tank: water level tells us when the outlet needs to change.
  • A slowly drifting level measurement can produce a persistent control error.
  • Wave energy converter: force and velocity determine mechanical power.
  • A timing error between channels can bias the power estimate.

Use the lab systems only as motivation. Do not explain the lab procedures. Ask whether a smooth trace must be an accurate trace.

Source: Analogue.pptx slides 2, 5; System Control.pptx slide 21

The measurement chain

Each stage can change the information that reaches the computer.

Read the chain from physical input to engineering result. Excitation supplies the sensor. Analogue filtering must precede digitisation when it is needed to prevent aliasing.

Source: Analogue.pptx slides 7, 20

Quantity, signal and measurement

StageExampleUnit
Physical quantityForce on the load cellN
Sensor outputSmall differential voltagemV
Conditioned signalAmplified voltageV
Reported measurementMass inferred from static forcekg
$$F=mg\qquad m=F/g$$

Distinguish mass and weight early. In the weighing exercise we report kilograms. Dividing by gravity is valid for a stationary object with the intended load path.

A strain-gauge load cell

  • Applied force deforms the elastic element.
  • Strain changes electrical resistance.
  • A bridge converts resistance changes into a small voltage.
  • Excitation and signal conditioning are required.

Avoid assuming a particular bridge topology for the actual equipment. The source figure is an illustration, not the specification of every load cell. Check the installed model and wiring.

Source: Analogue.pptx slide 9

Bridge excitation and differential output

$$V_{\mathrm{signal}}=V_+-V_-$$

The conditioner measures the voltage difference between the two output terminals.

A measurement bridge does not require a zero-current null measurement. Stable excitation matters because the output usually scales with excitation. Ratiometric systems can compensate for excitation variations.

Source: Analogue.pptx slides 9, 24

What does 2 mV/V mean?

Illustrative load cell: rated output 2 mV/V at full load, excitation 5 V.

$$V_{\mathrm{FS}}=(2\ \mathrm{mV/V})(5\ \mathrm{V})=10\ \mathrm{mV}$$

At half the rated load, the ideal output change is 5 mV.

mV/V is sensitivity normalised by excitation. It is not the gain of the conditioner. These numbers are a teaching example, not the specification of the supplied load cell.

Other sensors, different requirements

  • Wave gauge: water immersion changes the electrical response.
  • Pressure sensor: pressure becomes voltage or current.
  • Each sensor needs its own excitation, range and calibration.

A wave gauge can be affected by water conductivity. A pressure-derived level can be affected by pressure reference and fluid density. Sensor selection is secondary today.

Source: Analogue.pptx slides 8, 11

Why conditioning is needed

ProblemConditioning action
Only a few millivoltsAmplification
Output exceeds the DAQ rangeAttenuation or a suitable interface
Unwanted high-frequency contentAnalogue low-pass filtering
Sensor needs electrical powerExcitation
Different ground potentialsAppropriate grounding or isolation

Keep electrical conditioning distinct from calibration in software. An instrument may perform several of these operations internally.

Source: Analogue.pptx slides 20–27

Gain and offset

$$V_{\mathrm{out}}=G V_{\mathrm{sensor}}+V_{\mathrm{offset}}$$

Example: 0–10 mV sensor signal, 0–5 V conditioner output.

$$G=\frac{5}{0.010}=500$$

In practice, leave headroom for tare, overload and drift.

The nominal gain fills the range exactly. A smaller gain may be more robust. The tare load also consumes physical and electrical range. Amplifying sensor noise with the signal does not improve the input signal-to-noise ratio.

Source: Analogue.pptx slides 21, 27

Check: a clipped signal

A conditioner maps 0–10 kg to 0–5 V. A 12 kg load is applied and the output remains at 5 V.

Can software recover the mass?

No. Saturation has removed the information. Reduce gain or use a suitable sensor and input range.

Give pairs a minute before revealing the answer. No. Saturation has removed the information. Reduce gain or use a suitable sensor and input range.

A 4–20 mA signal

A suitable shunt resistor converts current into a measurable voltage.

$$V=IR\qquad R=250\ \Omega\quad\Rightarrow\quad 1\text{–}5\ \mathrm{V}$$
$$h=h_{\min}+\frac{I-4\ \mathrm{mA}}{16\ \mathrm{mA}}(h_{\max}-h_{\min})$$

Example: a 0–1 m level transmitter gives 12 mA at 0.5 m.

Check loop supply, transmitter compliance, resistor rating and DAQ grounding. For 20 mA and 250 ohm, dissipation is 0.1 W, so select an appropriate margin. Zero level is 4 mA. A broken loop is not automatically a zero-level measurement.

Calibration

Apply known inputs and record the resulting output.

$$V=a m+b\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad\hat m=\frac{V-b}{a}$$
  • Use several masses across the working range.
  • Repeat measurements and include unloading.
  • Keep one known mass aside for an independent check.

Fit voltage as a function of accurately known mass, then invert the relation. The slope has units V/kg and the intercept is in V. Calibration should include the complete assembled measurement chain.

Source: Analogue.pptx slides 12, 25, 29

Worked calibration

Mass [kg]Mean voltage [V]
0.00.10
0.51.10
1.02.10
1.53.10
$$a=2.00\ \mathrm{V/kg},\quad b=0.10\ \mathrm{V}$$
$$V=2.70\ \mathrm V\quad\Rightarrow\quad \hat m=1.30\ \mathrm{kg}$$

Ask students for the intercept first. Then calculate the slope from any pair. This exact synthetic data set illustrates the calculation. Real measurements will scatter.

Source: Adapted from the calibration task in Analogue.pptx slide 29

A fit needs an independent check

$$r_i=V_i-(a m_i+b)$$
  • Residuals should be small compared with the required measurement accuracy.
  • A curved pattern suggests a linear fit may be inadequate.
  • A held-out mass tests the calibration on new data.
  • Moving the mass across the plate checks position sensitivity.

R-squared alone is insufficient. Ask whether an apparently perfect fit through two points proves accuracy. A withheld mass and repeated placements answer different questions.

Accuracy and repeatability

ObservationPossible explanation
Repeated values scatter widelyNoise or unstable loading
Repeated values agree but are wrongCalibration bias
Zero changes over timeDrift or mounting change
Loading and unloading differHysteresis or mechanical friction

More averaging can reduce some random variation. It cannot repair a systematic calibration error. Drift may affect zero, sensitivity or both.

Source: Analogue.pptx slides 12, 50–51

Three load cells under one plate

$$\hat m_{\mathrm{object}}=\frac{F_1+F_2+F_3-F_{\mathrm{tare}}}{g}$$
  • All vertical support forces must pass through the load cells.
  • The plate’s weight is the tare.
  • Different cells may need different calibration coefficients.
  • Check centre and off-centre placements.

This retains the original three-cell exercise. If all channels have equal sensitivity, a sum-voltage calibration can work. Do not assume equal sensitivities. Use individual calibrations or a multichannel calibration with enough load positions.

Source: Analogue.pptx slide 70; Analogue.pdf page 57

Digitisation has two separate choices

Sampling
When do we measure?

$$T_s=1/f_s$$

Quantisation
Which digital level represents the voltage?

$$\Delta V\approx\frac{V_{\max}-V_{\min}}{2^n}$$

Sampling acts on time. Quantisation acts on amplitude. Neither choice guarantees overall measurement accuracy.

Source: Analogue.pptx slides 16–19

ADC resolution

More bits provide finer voltage steps.

Noise, calibration and drift still limit useful accuracy.

The drawing is qualitative. Avoid describing conversion as preserving all original information. Quantisation loses amplitude detail.

Source: Analogue.pptx slide 18

Worked resolution estimate

Illustrative 14-bit ADC with a ±10 V range and sensitivity 0.5 V/kg.

$$\Delta V=\frac{20}{16384}=1.22\ \mathrm{mV}$$
$$\Delta m=\frac{1.22\ \mathrm{mV}}{0.5\ \mathrm{V/kg}}=2.44\ \mathrm g$$

This is the nominal mass increment per code, not an accuracy claim.

Use the full 20 V span. The NI USB-6001 has a 14-bit ADC and a fixed ±10 V input range. Other devices differ. Conditioner range utilisation matters when the DAQ range cannot be changed.

Source: NI USB-6001 specifications: https://download.ni.com/support/manuals/374369a.pdf

Differential and single-ended inputs

ModeMeasured voltageTypical consideration
Single-endedSignal relative to DAQ groundGround differences enter the reading
DifferentialAI+ minus AI−Rejects some common-mode interference

Differential measurement still has common-mode voltage limits.

A differential input is not the same as galvanic isolation. Floating sources may require a bias-current return path. Use the device manual for channel pairing and wiring. Do not transfer the old slide’s channel numbers to another device.

Source: Analogue.pptx slides 32–33; NI USB-6001 specifications

Noise begins before the computer

  • Use the required cable and short signal paths where practical.
  • Keep low-level sensor wiring away from power and motor wiring.
  • Follow the equipment instructions for shields and grounding.
  • Check loose connections and mechanical vibration before filtering.

Avoid giving one universal shield-termination rule. The correct arrangement depends on equipment and interference. The central point is that software cannot replace correct wiring.

Source: Analogue.pptx slides 26, 32–33, 50

DAQ configuration

  • Identify the device and physical channels.
  • Match the terminal mode to the actual wiring.
  • Set the sampling rate and record length.
  • Inspect raw volts before applying calibration.
  • Save timestamps, units and the configuration with the data.

For multiple channels, check whether the specified rate is per channel or shared. Channel timing matters for products such as force times velocity. Keep the unfiltered data.

Source: Analogue.pptx slides 30–33

MATLAB acquisition example

devices = daqlist("ni");  % inspect device IDs first
d = daq("ni");
ch = addinput(d,"Dev1","ai0","Voltage");
ch.TerminalConfig = "Differential"; % match wiring
d.Rate = 1000;
raw = read(d,seconds(10));
t = seconds(raw.Time - raw.Time(1));
V = raw{:,1};
plot(t,V); xlabel("Time [s]"); ylabel("Voltage [V]");

Device ID is an example. Requires compatible NI hardware, drivers and MATLAB DAQ support.

Use the current DataAcquisition interface where supported. The uploaded lecture uses the older session interface. A legacy example is included in the exercise script. Confirm the lab installation before class.

Source: MathWorks addinput and read documentation; Analogue.pptx slide 31

Break

10 minutes

After the break: how fast should we sample, and how much should we filter?

Return at minute 70.

Sampling rate and record length

$$N=f_sT$$
ChoiceControls
Sampling rate fₛHighest frequency we can represent without aliasing
Record duration TSlow behaviour we can observe
Both togetherNumber of samples and data volume

A long record cannot repair an insufficient sampling rate.

For spectral analysis, the basic FFT frequency spacing is 1/T. This is optional detail. For a tank, the test must last long enough to see settling.

Source: Analogue.pptx slide 19

Aliasing

Different continuous signals can produce the same sampled values.

$$f_{\mathrm{alias}}=|f-kf_s|\quad\text{chosen in }[0,f_s/2]$$

Example: a 90 Hz component sampled at 100 Hz appears at 10 Hz.

For integer k choose the frequency folded into the Nyquist interval. Students can calculate 100 minus 90. Once sampled, the data cannot tell whether the original component was 10 or 90 Hz.

Source: Analogue.pptx slide 19

Nyquist is a limit, not a complete design

$$f_s>2f_{\max}$$
  • The condition assumes the input is band-limited.
  • A real analogue filter needs a transition band.
  • Sampling faster than the bare minimum makes filter design and timing easier.

Do not say equality at two samples per cycle is always sufficient. Phase can make a sine wave vanish at that boundary. Choose rates using both useful signal bandwidth and unwanted content.

Source: Analogue.pptx slide 19

Anti-aliasing belongs before the ADC

An analogue low-pass filter attenuates frequencies that would fold into the sampled band.

A digital filter works on values that have already been sampled.

If 90 Hz has become 10 Hz, a digital 10 Hz passband will retain it.

This is the main conceptual checkpoint. Some DAQ devices include useful anti-alias filtering and others do not. Verify the actual analogue front end.

Source: Analogue.pptx slides 19, 23, 63

Check: a slowly changing level

Useful level changes are below 1 Hz. Electrical interference is present at 50 Hz. You sample at 20 Hz.

Is the useful signal bandwidth alone enough to justify this setup?

No. The 50 Hz component aliases to 10 Hz unless attenuated before sampling. Check the analogue filter and leave a suitable transition band.

Give pairs a minute before revealing the answer. No. The 50 Hz component aliases to 10 Hz unless attenuated before sampling. Check the analogue filter and leave a suitable transition band.

What counts as noise?

  • Electrical pickup can create narrow peaks such as mains interference.
  • Mechanical vibration may be real but irrelevant to a static mass estimate.
  • Drift is slow and may survive a low-pass filter.
  • Random noise is not necessarily Gaussian, independent or zero mean.

Noise is defined relative to the measurement objective. Do not assume the central limit theorem makes every noise source white Gaussian noise.

Source: Analogue.pptx slides 50–51

Filter types

A static scale must retain the DC component that represents its mean load.

Ask which filter would destroy the static mass information. Answer: high-pass filtering removes the mean. The idealised edges in the image are not achievable exactly.

Source: Analogue.pptx slides 52–55

A first-order low-pass filter

$$RC\frac{dV_{\mathrm{out}}}{dt}+V_{\mathrm{out}}=V_{\mathrm{in}}$$
$$\tau=RC,\qquad f_c=\frac{1}{2\pi\tau}$$

Use capacitor storage as the physical intuition. The output cannot jump instantly. This first-order response will reappear in the tank lecture.

Source: Analogue.pptx slides 43, 59–60

Transfer function: a compact description

$$H(s)=\frac{V_{\mathrm{out}}(s)}{V_{\mathrm{in}}(s)}=\frac{1}{\tau s+1}$$
  • Valid for this linear model with zero initial conditions.
  • The same form describes many processes with storage.
  • A larger time constant gives a slower response.

Keep Laplace transforms to one slide. Explain that differentiation becomes multiplication by s when the initial conditions are zero. The appendix carries the extra theory.

Source: Analogue.pptx slides 34–44

Filtering changes amplitude and phase

$$|H(j2\pi f)|=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+(f/f_c)^2}}$$
$$\phi(f)=-\tan^{-1}(f/f_c)$$
FrequencyAmplitude ratioPhase
f = 0.1 f꜀0.995−5.7°
f = f꜀0.707−45°
f = 10 f꜀0.100−84.3°

The cutoff is the minus-three-decibel point for this filter. A cutoff ten times above the useful frequency reduces distortion but does not make the delay zero. Filtering in a feedback loop can affect stability.

Source: Analogue.pptx slides 45, 68

A simple digital smoother

$$y_k=(1-\alpha)y_{k-1}+\alpha x_k$$
$$\alpha=1-e^{-T_s/\tau}$$
  • Small α gives stronger smoothing and a slower response.
  • Initialise y with the first measurement.
  • This filter preserves a constant input after settling.

The formula comes from a first-order continuous filter with a piecewise constant input. It gives an intuitive implementation without filter-design toolboxes. It does not replace the analogue anti-alias filter.

Source: Analogue.pptx slides 63–69

Averaging a static mass

After the load has settled, estimate mass from a stable time window.

$$\bar m=\frac1N\sum_{k=1}^{N}m_k$$

For independent samples with standard deviation σ:

$$\sigma_{\bar m}=\sigma/\sqrt N$$

Filtered samples are correlated. The independent-sample formula then overstates the benefit. Repeating the placement tests more than taking many samples during one placement. Avoid averaging while the plate is still settling.

Filtering for weighing and control

Static weighingReal-time feedback
A stable window can be selected laterOnly past and present samples are available
Delay may be acceptableDelay can reduce control performance
Mean mass is the main resultBoth transient response and noise matter

Offline zero-phase filtering uses future data and cannot run causally in the same way.

Explain why a filter suitable for a final mass report may be unsuitable inside a fast controller. Force and velocity need compatible timing if they are used to calculate power.

Source: Analogue.pptx slide 68

Check: a very smooth wrong result

A scale repeatedly reports 1.08 kg for a 1.00 kg check mass. The scatter is only 0.002 kg.

Will stronger smoothing solve the problem?

No. Investigate tare, calibration, loading and drift. Small scatter demonstrates repeatability, not accuracy.

Give pairs a minute before revealing the answer. No. Investigate tare, calibration, loading and drift. Small scatter demonstrates repeatability, not accuracy.

Two-hour exercise

Exercise: the weighing challenge

Build and calibrate a scale. Estimate the mass of three unknown objects.

  • Keep the unknown objects out of the calibration data.
  • Submit the measurement code and a short procedure.
  • Report masses, units and repeatability.
  • Use the same final procedure for every object.

Two hours begin after the lecture. Groups should share roles for wiring, acquisition and analysis. The original task uses three load cells and three conditioners. Adapt only the hardware-specific channel configuration.

Source: Analogue.pptx slide 70; Analogue.pdf page 57

Two-hour exercise

Exercise timing

MinutesTask
0–15Mounting, load path and wiring check
15–40Calibration across the mass range
40–60Noise inspection and filter choice
60–80Independent mass and position checks
80–105Unknown objects with repeated placements
105–120Results, code and method submission

Do not let groups spend the whole exercise tuning a filter. Require a raw voltage plot by minute 15 and a calibration by minute 40.

Two-hour exercise

Exercise 1: mounting and raw data

  • Check capacity, excitation and conditioner output range.
  • Verify that each cell responds with the expected sign.
  • Record the unloaded plate for 10 seconds.
  • Apply a known mass and inspect all channels.
  • Save the raw recording before further processing.

Do not apply a load beyond the actual cell capacity. If a channel clips or does not change, solve that problem before fitting a calibration.

Two-hour exercise

Exercise 2: calibration and validation

  • Calibrate each cell separately using known vertical loads.
  • Repeat each placement at least three times.
  • Use four mass levels including zero. Assemble and tare the plate.
  • Check an independent known mass at several plate positions.
  • Report calibration coefficients with units.

Use four calibration levels including zero and reserve a known mass for validation. Calibrate each cell with the known vertical load through that cell, preserving its intended loading direction and conditioner settings. Do not assign the total plate mass to each supporting cell. After assembly, sum the calibrated forces, subtract plate tare and check several load positions. A combined regression is an alternative only with enough independent load positions to identify channel sensitivities.

Two-hour exercise

Exercise 3: noise and reporting

  • Plot a raw trace and an amplitude spectrum of a stationary interval.
  • Choose smoothing that retains the mean and allows settling.
  • Estimate each unknown mass from at least three placements.
  • Report the mean and spread across placements.
  • Explain the largest remaining source of error.

The MATLAB starter includes a basic FFT plot. Removing the mean before the FFT helps inspect fluctuations but must not remove the mean used for weighing.

Two-hour exercise

The scoring rule

$$J=\frac{100}{3}\sum_{i=1}^{3}\frac{|\hat m_i-m_{i,\mathrm{ref}}|}{m_{i,\mathrm{ref}}}$$

Lowest mean absolute percentage error wins.

Also submit a calibration plot, validation result and reproducible code.

Proposed scoring rule, clarified from the original cumulative normalised error. The reference masses remain with the instructor. Relative scoring gives equal proportional importance to each object. A winner still needs a defensible method.

Optional material

Optional: linear and time-invariant

$$H[a x_1+b x_2]=aH[x_1]+bH[x_2]$$
  • Linear: superposition holds.
  • Time-invariant: shifting the input in time shifts the output by the same amount.
  • Clipping, dead zones and changing parameters break these assumptions.

Optional after the exercise or if students ask about the transfer function. Real devices often behave approximately linearly only over a limited range.

Source: Analogue.pptx slides 34–39

Optional material

Optional: FIR and IIR filters

FIRIIR
Finite impulse-response durationImpulse response can continue indefinitely
Moving average is one exampleExponential smoother is one example
Finite coefficients give BIBO stabilityFeedback coefficients must ensure stability
Linear phase possible with symmetric coefficientsPhase behaviour depends on the design

Avoid the source claim that FIR filters simply have no poles. Also avoid a blanket claim that digital filters are slower than analogue filters. Latency depends on design and implementation.

Source: Analogue.pptx slides 63–67

Optional material

Optional: a MATLAB filter comparison

Fs = 1000;
t = (0:1/Fs:5-1/Fs)';
x = 1 + 0.1*sin(2*pi*50*t) + 0.02*randn(size(t));
tau = 0.1; alpha = 1-exp(-1/(Fs*tau));
y = zeros(size(x)); y(1) = x(1);
for k = 2:numel(x)
    y(k) = (1-alpha)*y(k-1) + alpha*x(k);
end
plot(t,x,t,y); legend("Raw","Filtered");

Compare the settled means. Then replace the constant input with a step.

Uses base MATLAB. The signal is synthetic. The smoother is causal. Compare noise reduction against settling time.

Source: Adapted from Analogue.pptx slide 69
